newsitem.title: CHINA: Shipping tycoon to be candidate for chief HK exec.
newsitem.headline: Shipping tycoon to be candidate for chief HK exec.

text.p: Hong Kong shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, long touted as a frontrunner for Hong Kong's top job after it reverts to Chinese rule next year, has formally become a candidate for the post, Chinese officials said on Friday.
"He is one of those on the list of candidates," said a spokesman for the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office under the State Council, or cabinet.

"He has the intention of running for chief executive," the spokesman said as China's Preparatory Committee handling the British colony's 1997 return to Beijing rule ended the first day of a two-day session.

Members of the committee were meeting in Beijing to propose the names of favoured candidates for the much-coveted seats on the Selection Committee that will choose the chief executive, another official said.
"This time the committee members will put forward the candidates they have their eyes on," said Kang Guowei, an official with the State Council's Hong Kong affairs office.
Kang declined to give details of nominees or what criteria the Preparatory Committee would use in the final selection.
Tung had said last month he was a likely candidate but said he would make a final decision based on the composition of the selection committee.
Many in Hong Kong believe Beijing signalled it favoured Tung in January when President Jiang Zemin singled him out from a group of Hong Kong advisers for a vigorous handshake.

Four other candidates to declare their interest in the job are former Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang, former Hong Kong cabinet member Lo Tak-shing, businessman Peter Woo, and former High Court judge Arthur Garcia.

The Preparatory Committee was expected to meet in early or mid-November to choose the final 400 members of the Selection Committee and within two months would name its choice for the first chief executive of Hong Kong under Chinese rule, the spokesman said.

Chairman of the Preparatory Committee and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said he hoped the committee would strive to make choices on merit and ensure the future panel had a good balance of candidates from all walks of life.

The official Xinhua news agency quoted Qian as saying he hoped "every committee member will embrace a spirit of responsibility and choose the worthy and able... and put forth suitable recommendations".

In September, nearly 6,000 Hong Kong residents applied for a place on the panel, which will pick the first person to lead the British colony after the territory reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Qian said the unexpectedly high number of applications proved that most of the territory's residents had confidence in Beijing's handling of the handover.

"Hong Kong people from all walks of life enthusiastically participated in applying for the Selection Committee, illustrating that the broad mass of Hong Kong people love China and love Hong Kong," Qian said.
